title: CSRF, SameSite cookies and where the session lives
objectives: Explain how CSRF works — the browser attaches cookies to a request another site starts — and why a bearer-token API isn't exposed the same way
Predict whether a cookie is sent cross-site under `SameSite=Strict`, `Lax` and `None`, and which browsers apply `Lax` when the attribute is missing
Write a server-side guard that rejects cross-site state-changing requests with `Sec-Fetch-Site`, an exact `Origin` fallback, and fail-closed handling of missing headers
Explain what Next.js Server Actions check (POST only, `Origin` vs host, `allowedOrigins`) and what they leave to you
Choose where the session token lives — `HttpOnly` cookie or `localStorage` — by what an XSS can do with each

sources.title: OWASP Cheat Sheet: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention
OWASP Cheat Sheet: HTML5 Security (Local Storage)
Next.js docs: Data Security (Server Actions, allowed origins)

questions.prompt: A page on `evil.example` mounts a CSRF attack on your cookie-authenticated app. What can it actually do?

options.text: Make the victim's browser send a state-changing request that carries the victim's cookies — without being able to read the response
Read the victim's data from your API's responses
Copy the victim's session cookie to its own server
Run JavaScript inside your origin

questions.explanation: CSRF borrows the browser's habit of attaching cookies by destination. The attacker chooses the request, and the browser adds the credentials, but the same-origin policy still stops `evil.example` reading the response, and the cookie value never leaves the browser. That's why CSRF targets actions (transfer, change email, delete) rather than data. Running script inside your origin is XSS, a different and worse bug.

questions.prompt: Your SPA's API authenticates only with an `Authorization: Bearer …` header that your own JavaScript adds to each `fetch`. A cross-site page auto-submits a form to that API. What happens?

options.text: The request arrives without the header, so it's unauthenticated: the browser never adds that header on its own
The browser forwards the `Authorization` header like a cookie, so the forgery succeeds
It succeeds unless the API's responses set `SameSite`
CORS blocks the form submission before it's sent

questions.explanation: CSRF needs credentials the *browser* attaches automatically — cookies, or HTTP authentication the browser remembers. A bearer token your code adds isn't one, so a page on another site can't make it appear. (That's a property of the token's transport, covered in `auth-over-http`; the trade-off is the XSS exposure of wherever you keep the token.) `SameSite` is a cookie attribute and doesn't apply. CORS doesn't block sending a form at all; it governs reading responses.

questions.prompt: Your session cookie is set without a `SameSite` attribute. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Chromium browsers treat it as `Lax`; Firefox (by default) and Safari don't, so for their users it rides cross-site requests — set it explicitly
Every major browser has defaulted to `Lax` since 2020, so it's protected everywhere
Browsers default to `Strict`, which is the safest choice
Modern browsers reject a cookie without `SameSite`

questions.explanation: Chrome made `Lax` the default in Chrome 80 (2020), and Edge followed. MDN's compat data lists Firefox's Lax-by-default only behind a preference, and Safari not at all. An unlabelled cookie is therefore protected for some users and not others, and even in Chromium the default comes with a two-minute window in which cross-site `POST`s still carry it. Label it.

questions.prompt: The app is on `https://app.example.com`, with a `SameSite=Strict` session cookie. User uploads are served from `https://uploads.example.com`. An uploaded HTML page auto-submits a form to the app. Is the cookie sent?

options.text: Yes. Both share the registrable domain `example.com`, so the request is same-site and `SameSite` doesn't restrict it
No. `Strict` blocks every request from a different host
No. The two have different origins, and `SameSite` compares origins
Only if the form uses `GET`

questions.explanation: For `SameSite`, a site is the scheme plus the registrable domain, so sibling subdomains are the same site even though they're different origins. `Strict` only withholds the cookie on cross-*site* requests. This is the gap a server-side check closes: the browser reports `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site`, and a guard that accepts only `same-origin` rejects it.

questions.prompt: A `POST` to a cookie-authenticated endpoint arrives with neither `Sec-Fetch-Site` nor `Origin`. What does OWASP's CSRF cheat sheet say to do?

options.text: Reject it unless another defence, such as a valid CSRF token, passes: missing headers aren't evidence of a same-origin request
Allow it: every modern browser sends `Origin` on a `POST`, so it must be `curl`, which can't carry the victim's cookies
Allow it if the `User-Agent` looks like a real browser
Treat it as a `GET` and let it through

questions.explanation: OWASP: "Missing headers and Origin: null are not evidence of a same-origin request" — fail closed unless something else proves the request is genuine. The "must be curl" reasoning is real: it's the trade-off Next.js makes for Server Actions, which let a request with no `Origin` through with a warning. But it's a judgment about which clients exist, and OWASP's default is stricter. `User-Agent` is set by whoever sends the request, and a method label changes nothing about what the handler does.

questions.prompt: What does Next.js 16 do on its own to protect Server Actions from CSRF?

options.text: Accepts them only as `POST`, and aborts the action when the `Origin` header's host doesn't match `Host`/`X-Forwarded-Host` (or an `allowedOrigins` entry)
Embeds a hidden CSRF token in every form that uses an action
Forces `SameSite=Strict` on every cookie the app sets
Nothing is needed: action IDs are encrypted, so another site can't call an action

questions.explanation: The data security guide describes both: actions can only be invoked with `POST`, and "Server Actions in Next.js also compare the Origin header to the Host header (or X-Forwarded-Host). If these don't match, the request will be aborted." There's no token, and Next.js doesn't rewrite your cookie attributes. Action IDs are non-deterministic, but an attacker can read them from your page like any other markup, and the guide still says to treat actions as reachable via direct POST.

questions.prompt: Which of these gets no origin check from Next.js, even though it accepts cookie-authenticated `POST`s?

options.text: A `POST` function exported from `app/api/transfer/route.ts`
A Server Action passed to `<form action={transfer}>`
A Server Action called through `useActionState`
A Server Action imported into a Client Component and called from an event handler

questions.explanation: The origin comparison is part of how Next.js handles Server Actions, however they're invoked: form, `useActionState` or a direct call from client code. A Route Handler is your own HTTP endpoint, and Next.js documents no such check for it. If it authenticates with cookies, add the `Sec-Fetch-Site`/`Origin` guard yourself.

questions.prompt: You're choosing between an `HttpOnly` session cookie and a token in `localStorage` sent as a bearer header. Which comparison is accurate?

options.text: `localStorage` removes CSRF but lets any XSS read the token and use it elsewhere until it expires; the `HttpOnly` cookie needs CSRF defences, and an XSS can act through it only while the tab is open
An `HttpOnly` cookie makes the app immune to XSS
`localStorage` is encrypted per origin, so injected script can't read it
They're equivalent: an XSS can steal either one

questions.explanation: OWASP's HTML5 cheat sheet: "Do not store session identifiers in local storage as the data is always accessible by JavaScript." An `HttpOnly` cookie can't be read by script, so it can't be exfiltrated. But it's not XSS immunity: the injected script can still call your API, and the browser attaches the cookie. `localStorage` isn't encrypted or shielded from scripts on the same origin. The cookie trades XSS token theft for CSRF exposure, and CSRF has cheap, reliable defences.

prompts.prompt: Set a session cookie the browser will only accept with `Secure`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`; hide it from page script; and say explicitly that cross-site POSTs mustn't carry it.
prompts.explanation: The `__Host-` prefix makes the browser reject the cookie unless it's `Secure`, has `Path=/` and has no `Domain` (MDN), which locks it to this exact host. `HttpOnly` keeps `document.cookie` (and so an XSS) from reading it. `SameSite=Lax` withholds it from cross-site `POST`s, and `Strict` from all cross-site requests. Write it out, because only Chromium applies `Lax` by default.

prompts.prompt: Finish the check for a state-changing request: trust Fetch Metadata first, fall back to an exact `Origin` match, and fail closed.
prompts.explanation: `Sec-Fetch-Site` is set by the browser and can't be changed by page script; accepting only `same-origin` excludes sibling subdomains (`same-site`). For browsers without it, `Origin` must equal a trusted origin exactly: `includes` on an array of full origins, never `startsWith`. With neither header there's no evidence, so the request is refused.

prompts.prompt: Your Next.js 16 app sits behind a proxy whose public host is `my-proxy.com`, and the proxy doesn't forward that host. Let Server Actions accept requests from it and its subdomains.
prompts.explanation: `allowedOrigins` lists extra hosts whose `Origin` may invoke actions. Entries match the origin's host (plus port if present), and `*` covers exactly one label, so the bare `my-proxy.com` needs its own entry. If the proxy forwards the public host in `X-Forwarded-Host`, no entry is needed at all.

snippets.question: How many origins does the prefix check accept?
snippets.explanation: `startsWith` accepts the real origin, and also `app.example.com.evil.test` (a domain anyone can register) and the same host on another port, which is a different origin that may be a different service. Only `"null"` fails. An origin is an exact triple of scheme, host and port, so compare the whole string: `origin === trusted`, or an array's `includes(origin)` against a list of full origins. (Not `trusted.includes(origin)` on a single string: that's a substring test, and it accepts `https://app.example.co`.)

snippets.question: What three booleans are printed?
snippets.explanation: `*` matches exactly one non-empty label, so `*.my-proxy.com` matches `app.my-proxy.com` but neither the bare `my-proxy.com` (no label to match) nor `eu.app.my-proxy.com` (two labels). That's why the docs list `my-proxy.com` and `*.my-proxy.com` as two entries, and why `**.my-proxy.com` exists for deeper subdomains. (This imports an internal Next.js module to show the behaviour; in an app you only write the config.)
